name: Dusky mauve
lede: Livid Purple is a dusky, muted purple from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, one of the rarest colors in our painting archive, though a matching hue turns up in a Bronzino portrait painted 367 years before the name existed.

sections.title: A tight match across three books
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas carries this tone on plate XXXVII, hue 63″, notated 0.8RP 4.5/4.7 in the Munsell system [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary groups it under block 245, naming it grayish reddish purple, only 1.6 units from Ridgway's reading, one of the tighter matches in this naming lineage [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists the same swatch independently, cited in the same 1955 circular [2].

Its closest neighbor in our library is [[livid-violet]], about 3.1 units away and more purple, followed by [[dull-purple]], about 4.0 units off and more vivid [3]. [[light-perilla-purple]] and [[claret-cup]] sit a little further, about 4.4 to 4.6 units off and redder [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive matches this tone in only 15 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.06 percent, as photographed, rarer than 69 percent of the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.3 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 3.8 times its museums' expected rate [4].

The earliest match in the archive is a 1545 portrait by Bronzino, 367 years before the name itself was recorded in 1912, a reminder that the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of any pigment or dye, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. The third-earliest dated match is 1869, and the latest is 1941, across only 11 dated paintings in total [4].
